en: Outline and Compendium of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Volume One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yongguang of Guangde Monastery in Suining;
verified by the Śramaṇa Weijing of Songfeng Monastery in Renshou.
I prostrate with my head touching the feet of the Lord Vairocana of the Avataṃsaka, the Great Teacher of the Flower Treasury Adornment,
the bodhisattvas of the ten directions as numerous as motes of dust, the devas, nāgas, and spirit kings who protect the Dharma,
and all the sages and worthies gathered in the ocean-like assembly of the Dharma realm. I now pay homage to you all with my head meeting your feet.
May the majestic spiritual power of the Triple Gem Empower all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm Who see,
hear, read, recite, or transcribe this, So that they may all attain Buddhahood and transcend to the other shore.
Now, by the slight power of my single thought, May I universally benefit all sentient beings submerged in saṃsāra.
The single true Dharma-realm, the nature of True Suchness, Is pure, adorned, and wondrous beyond compare;
Realized by sages yet unfathomable to the minds of ordinary beings, Its myriad practices perfected, it is inconceivable.
I shall now record, one by one, the five weeks, four divisions, seven locations, and nine assemblies that follow.

The First Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment. Samantabhadra serves as the presiding master of the assembly. He expounds upon the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s reliance on both the primary and secondary [bodies].
The Buddha emits light from his mouth and light from between his eyebrows. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Vairocana-garbha-kāya-samādhi.
This comprises six chapters: Chapter One, "The Sublime Array of World Rulers"; Chapter Two, "The Tathāgata Manifesting Signs"; Chapter Three, "Samantabhadra’s Samādhi."
Three. Chapter Four: The Accomplishment of the World; Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World; Chapter Six: Vairocana.
These six chapters of the sutra constitute the Section on Faith, which constitutes the cycle of the causes and effects of that which is to be believed.

The second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*), with Mañjuśrī serving as the presiding master. Therein he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). The Buddha emitted light from the wheels on his two feet;
this assembly did not enter meditative absorption. It comprises six chapters: Chapter Seven, "The Names and Titles of the Tathāgata";
Chapter Eight, "The Four Noble Truths" (*catur-āryasatya*); Chapter Nine, "Awakening through Light"; Chapter Ten, "The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination"; and Chapter [Eleven], "Pure Conduct."
Chapter Eleven. Chapter Twelve: Samantabhadra. Third Assembly at the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Dharmamati serves as the presiding master of the assembly and expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*). The Buddha emits light from the two toes of his feet;
the Bodhisattva Dharmamati enters the Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means. These comprise six chapters. Ascending Mount Sumeru.
Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on the Summit (Cūḍā-paṭala). Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on the Praise in Gāthās of Mount Sumeru. Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Ten Abodes (Daśabhūmi-paṭala).

Chapter Sixteen: The Chapter on the Holy Life (Brahmacarya-paṭala). Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment (Prathamacittotpāda-guṇa-paṭala). Chapter Eighteen: The Chapter on the Clarification of the Dharma (Dharmavyakti-paṭala).
The Fourth Assembly, in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. Guṇakūṭa serves as the presiding master of the assembly and expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices.
The Buddha emits light from the two soles of his feet, and Guṇakūṭa enters the Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation. [These comprise] four chapters:
Chapter Nineteen, "Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven"; Chapter Twenty, "Praise in Verses by the Yāmas"; and Chapter Twenty-one, "The Ten Practices."
The Twenty-second Chapter: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries (*Daśākṣayastūpa-kośa*).
The Fifth Assembly at the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. Vajradhvaja is the presiding master of the assembly. He expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications (*Daśapariṇāmanā*).
The Buddha emits light from the wheels on both his knees. The Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja enters the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom. [These comprise] three sections in total.
Chapter Twenty-three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. Chapter Twenty-four: Verses of Praise in Tuṣita.
Chapter Twenty-five: The Ten Dedications.
The sixth assembly was held in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Vajragarbha served as the presiding master and expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*).
The Buddha emitted light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, and the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom.
This constitutes a single fascicle: Chapter Twenty-six, the "Ten Stages."

The seventh assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance. The Tathāgata served as the presiding master of the assembly and expounded the Dharma-gates of Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment.
The Buddha emitted light from his brow and light from his mouth; the Buddha entered the *kṣaṇa-samādhi*. These comprise eleven chapters:
Chapter Twenty-seven, "The Ten Samādhis"; Chapter Twenty-eight, "The Ten Supernatural Powers"; Chapter Twenty-nine, "The Ten Endurances"; and Chapter Thirty, "The *Asaṃkhyeya*."
Chapter Thirty: On Lifespan; Chapter Thirty-one: On the Abodes of Bodhisattvas; Chapter Thirty-two:

On the Dwellings of Bodhisattvas—these twenty-six chapters constitute the Section on Exposition (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*), which distinguishes the cycle of causes and effects. Chapter Thirty-three: On the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha;
Chapter Thirty-four: On the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies; Chapter [Thirty-five]: On the Radiance of the Minor Marks.
Chapter Thirty-Five. Chapter Thirty-Six: The Conduct of Samantabhadra (this chapter on Samantabhadra is titled "The Cause of Equality"). Chapter Thirty-Seven:
The Manifestation of the Tathāgata (the chapter on the manifestation of the Tathāgata is titled "The Fruit of Equality").
The Eighth Assembly, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, has Samantabhadra as the presiding master. It expounds two thousand gates of practice. This assembly does not emit light.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Buddha’s Flower Adornment Samādhi. Together, this constitutes one fascicle. Chapter Thirty-Eight: Leaving the World (*Lokottara-varga*).
This chapter belongs to the Section on Practice (*caryā-bhāga*), serving to complete the cycle of the causes and effects of practice.
The Ninth Assembly at Jetavana. The Tathāgata’s Good Friend acts as the presiding host of the assembly, preaching the Dharmadhātu of the Fruit.

The Buddha emits a ray of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, which enters the "Entering the Dharmadhātu" Chapter, the thirty-ninth. This chapter constitutes the Section of Realization (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the realization of the cycle of cause and fruit, it is collectively termed the "Five Cycles": first, the Cycle of Cause and Fruit of Faith; second, the Cycle of Differentiated Cause and Fruit; third...
The cycle of equal cause and effect; the cycle of the fourfold accomplishment of practice; and the cycle of realization and entry—these are collectively termed the Four Divisions:
first, the Division of Faith; second, the Division of Understanding; third, the Division of Practice; and fourth, the Division of Realization.
Therefore, it is named the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Scripture of the One Vehicle, Perfect Teaching, consisting of seven locations, nine assemblies, five cycles, and four divisions.

Furthermore, in the first assembly, the Tathāgata’s reliance upon the gateways of the True Dharma was taught, signifying the Tathāgata’s reliance upon the primary and secondary adornments at the aranya site of the Bodhimaṇḍa;
this shall be clarified later in the sutra itself.

In the second assembly, at the Hall of Universal Radiance, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths. As for the Ten Faiths, they are ten kinds of faith: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness;
third, the mind of wisdom; fourth, the mind of diligence; fifth, the mind of concentration; sixth, the mind of non-retrogression; seventh, the mind of dedication;
eighth, the mind of protecting the Dharma; ninth, the mind of precepts; and tenth, the compliant mind. The functions of these ten minds shall be explained later in the sutra.
This is self-evident.
At the third assembly, in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes. As for the Ten Abodes: first, the Abode of Initial Resolve;

second, the Abode of Purifying the Ground; third, the Abode of Cultivating Practice; fourth, the Abode of Noble Birth; fifth, the Abode of Perfecting Skillful Means; sixth, the Abode of Rectifying the Mind.
Seventh is the stage of non-retrogression; eighth is the stage of youthful truth; ninth is the stage of the Dharma Prince; tenth is the stage of consecration.
The functional efficacy of these ten stages will be clarified by the sutra itself later on.

In the fourth assembly, at the palace of the Yāma Heaven, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices. As for the ten practices: first, the practice of joy; second, the practice of benefiting others;
third, the practice of non-opposition; fourth, the practice of being unbending; fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion;

sixth, the practice of skillful manifestation; seventh, the practice of non-attachment; eighth, the practice that is difficult to attain; ninth, the practice of wholesome dharmas; tenth, the practice of reality. These are the ten practices.
The efficacy of the Dharma shall be clarified later in the sutra itself.
In the fifth assembly, at the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). As for the Ten Dedications:

first, the dedication that rescues and protects all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being"; second, the indestructible dedication; third, the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
1. Dedication; 2. Dedication of the roots of goodness that are inexhaustible; 3. Dedication for the sake of all sentient beings; 4. Dedication reaching all places; 5.
Dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit; 6. Dedication entering into the equality of all roots of goodness; 7. Dedication that equally accords with all sentient beings;
8. Dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*); 9. Dedication of liberation without attachment or bondage; 10. Dedication entering the inexhaustibility of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The efficacy of these ten methods of dedication shall be clarified later in the sūtra itself.

In the sixth assembly, at the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) was taught. As for the Ten Grounds: first, the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);

second, the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*); third, the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*); fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*); fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*); sixth, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*); seventh, the Ground of Distance...

The Stage of Practice; the Eighth, the Immovable Stage; the Ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the Tenth, the Cloud of Dharma Stage. The functional application of these ten stages will be clarified later in the sūtra itself.

Seventh, they meet again in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍala*). There, the Tathāgata expounds for them the Dharma-gate of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyak-saṃbodhi*).

Regarding "Equal Enlightenment": this refers to the stage following the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), namely the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Having entered the position of Equal Enlightenment, one receives the office of a Buddha;

one's merit is equal to that of a Buddha because the practice of awakening is perfected. Regarding "Wondrous Enlightenment": this refers to the wondrously luminous nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*), which is no different from that of a Buddha. Its merit is equal to the fruit of Buddhahood. It is... [incomparable].
Because there is no distinction between the two, from the tenth stage to the eleventh stage there is no effortful exertion, as the position has reached the ultimate fruit.
(This assembly is held in the Heaven of the Eight Dhyānas; the scriptural text has not yet reached that point.)
In the third assembly, at the Hall of Universal Radiance, Samantabhadra served as the presiding master and expounded two thousand gates of practice.

Following two hundred questions posed by the Bodhisattva Samantamati, he explained such matters as: "What is the reliance of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? What constitutes their extraordinary excellence?"
What is practice? What is a spiritual friend? What is diligent vigor? What is the mind attaining peace and security?
What is maturing sentient beings? What is ethical discipline? What is knowing for oneself that one has received the prediction of enlightenment?
What is entering the stage of a bodhisattva? What is entering the stage of a Tathāgata? And what is sitting at the site of enlightenment?
At that time, he manifested extraordinary signs. For what reason did he demonstrate the subduing of Māra? What constitutes the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s powers?
How does one turn the wheel of Dharma and attain the pure dharmas? For what reason did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifest parinirvāṇa?
"Excellent, O Son of the Buddha! We pray that you will expound upon such dharmas as these. In total, there are two hundred questions within this dharma-gate. This...
The twenty questions from beginning to end are briefly listed by title; they are fully contained within the sutra itself.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, such as Samantamati Bodhisattva: "O Sons of the Buddha!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of reliance, ten kinds of wonders, ten kinds of practices,
ten kinds of spiritual friends, ten kinds of diligent exertion, ten kinds of mental peace and security, ten kinds of ways to mature sentient beings, ten kinds of precepts,

ten kinds of self-knowledge regarding the reception of the prediction of enlightenment, and ten kinds of entry into the bodhisattvas. By means of these, the bodhisattva universally enters [into all things].
Regarding the three periods of time, the Tathāgata—up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—manifests parinirvāṇa because he contemplates ten meanings.
Based on the aforementioned scriptural passages, there is one category of question for each, answered by means of ten [meanings]. In total, there are two thousand dharma-gates of response;
therefore, it is called "the Two Thousand Responses of the Pitcher. This shall be clarified later in the sūtra itself.

The ninth assembly was held in the Jeta Grove. The Tathāgata’s Good Friend served as the presiding host of the assembly and taught the Dharma-realm of fruition, titled the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm.
As for the Tathāgata’s Good Friends, they are Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya; these three are they.

Mañjuśrī, residing in the Great Jewel-Adorned Well-Situated Pavilion in the Jeta Grove, took leave of the Buddha and traveled southward, together with boundless [bodhisattvas] from the ten directions.
The great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas from the oceans of lands traveled together toward the south.
Passing through the human realm, they arrived at the eastern side of the City of Blessings and stayed at a great stupa within the Śāla Grove of the Banner of Adornment.

There, Mañjuśrī, together with the bodhisattvas who had come with him, was preaching the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*, in which the fundamental wisdom is luminously penetrating and all-pervasive. Following...
Because its roots are all-pervasive, it has one hundred million *nayuta* of unspeakable numbers of *sūtras* as its retinue.
It exhorts all bodhisattvas to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, to the east of Puṇyavatī City, there were five hundred *upāsakas*, headed by Mahāmati; five hundred *upāsikās*, headed by Mahāprajñā; and five hundred youths...
With Sudhana at their head, five hundred young women, with Samantabhadra at their head, went to the place where Mañjuśrī was.
Having completed their acts of reverence, they each sat to one side. Mañjuśrī observed the roots of goodness and the causal conditions of Sudhana and expounded various essential teachings.
Having heard them, Sudhana received them with joy and veneration. Sudhana then asked: "First, regarding the arousal of the mind toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
[Regarding] the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: how does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? How does one practice the bodhisattva conduct?
Mañjuśrī directed Sudhana to travel south to the country of Supratiṣṭhita, to the mountain Meghadri, to the presence of the bhikṣu Meghaśrī, saying, "He shall explain this for you.
From that point onward, [Sudhana] passed through one hundred and ten cities and fifty-three [teachers] who were well-versed in the knowledge.
Regarding the places where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī inquired about the Dharma of practice, each expounded a Dharma-gate; these shall be clarified in their respective chapters later on.
As for the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the primary spiritual friend is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who presides over fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

The first spiritual friend, the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, presides over the first stage among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), namely, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-bhūmi*). Regarding these...
He attained a liberation door called "The Universal Vision of the Wisdom-Light of the Realm of All Buddhas through Mindfulness.
The second spiritual friend was the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha from the country of Samudramukha;
he presided over the Dwelling of the Earth, and the liberation door he attained was called "The Universal Eye. The third spiritual friend was [the one from] the village of Samudratīra.

The bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita dwells in the practice of cultivation; the gate of liberation he has attained is called the "Unobstructed Gate of Liberation for Universally and Swiftly Making Offerings to All Buddhas and Accomplishing Sentient Beings.

The fourth spiritual friend, the elder Megha of the country of Dharṇicīta, presides over the stage of Noble Birth; the gate of liberation he has attained is called the "Mantra of the Sublime Bodhisattva."
The Dharma-door of the Radiance of the Bhikṣuṇī. Fifth is the Householder Liberation Master Forest-Dweller of the City of Good Knowledge, who dwells in the perfection of skillful means.
The liberation door he has attained is named the "Liberation Door of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Adornment."
The sixth spiritual friend is the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha of the border of Jambudvīpa, who presides over the stage of Abiding in the Rectitude of Mind.
The dharma-gate of liberation he has attained is called the Dharma-Gate of the Radiance of the Samādhis of the Ten Prajñāpāramitās.
The seventh spiritual friend is the upāsikā Śrīmati of the Sea-Tide, who presides over the stage of Non-Retrogression. The dharma-gate of liberation she has attained is called...
The eighth spiritual friend was the seer Samudrareṇu at the site of the ocean tide;
he presided over the stage of the youthful prince (*kumārabhūmi*) and attained the liberation door named "the Bodhisattva’s Invincible Banner.
The ninth spiritual friend was the brahmin Jvalanānta in the village of Īśāna; he presided over the stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarājaputra*). The [liberation door] he attained...
He attained a liberation door called the Bodhisattva’s Inexhaustible Wheel Liberation Door. The tenth spiritual friend was the girl Maitrāyaṇī of the city of Siṃhavijṛmbhita;
she presided over the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka). The liberation door she attained was called the Universal Adornment Gate of Prajñāpāramitā.
These ten spiritual friends preside over the dharma-gates of the ten stages (daśabhūmi). Their merit—
The practice of the Dharma will be clarified later in the sutra itself.
Twenty: The Chapter on the Dharma-Gates of the Ten Good Spiritual Friends. First: The Good Spiritual Friend, the Bhikṣu Sudarśana of the Land of Trinetra, who presides over the Practice of Joy.
The Dharma-gate he has attained is named the Bodhisattva’s Liberation Gate of the Lamp of Accordance.
The second spiritual friend was the youth Sovereign of the Land of Fame; he presided over the practice of beneficial conduct.
The Dharma-gate he attained is called the Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Great Supernatural Powers and Wisdom in All Arts and Crafts.

The third spiritual friend was the laywoman Endowed with Perfection in the City of Ocean Abode; she presided over the practice of non-opposing conduct. The Dharma-gate she attained is called the Inexhaustible...
The liberation door of the treasury of merit. The fourth spiritual friend was the wise layman Mahāudyānapura, who presides over unyielding conduct.
The dharma door he has attained is named the liberation door of the treasury of merit produced at will.
The fifth spiritual friend was the elder Ratnaśikhin of the city of Siṃhala; he presided over conduct free from delusion and confusion.
The Dharma gate he attained is called the Bodhisattva’s Liberation Gate of the Inexhaustible Jewel-Treasury of Merit.

The sixth spiritual friend was the elder Samantanetra of the land of Vīraṇamūla; he presided over the practice of the Well-Appearing. The Dharma gate he attained is called that which causes all sentient beings...
The seventh spiritual friend was King Never-Tiring of the city of Tārā-dhvaja;
he presided over the practice of non-attachment and attained the dharma-gate called the Door of Liberation Like an Illusion.

The eighth spiritual friend was King Great Light of the city of Suvarṇaprabhāsa; he presided over the practice that is difficult to attain and attained the dharma-gate called the Bodhisattva’s Great... [Dhāraṇī].
The samādhi liberation door of "Compassion as the Foremost, Accordant with the World.
Ninth is the laywoman Anācalā, Queen of the City of Abiding in Good Friends, who presides over the practice of wholesome dharmas;
the dharma door she has attained is named the "Samādhi Radiance Liberation Door of Seeking All Dharmas Without Weariness. Tenth is the laywoman of the city of Tuṣāra.
The renunciant outsider ascetic, Master of True Practice, attained a dharma gate called the Bodhisattva’s Gate of Liberation Reaching All Places.
Thus, these ten spiritual friends preside over the ten gates of practice; such is the efficacy of practicing these dharmas.
This shall be explained in detail later.
Regarding the third *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) gate, the ten spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): the first spiritual friend is the Elder Mahāgovinda, the Perfumer of the City.
He presides over the dedication of "Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings. The dharma attained therein is as follows:
The gate is named the Liberation Gate of the Method for Harmonizing Fragrances. The second spiritual friend is the captain Po-shi-lo (Vasula) of the city of the pavilion;
he presides over indestructible dedication. The Dharma gate he has attained is named the Liberation Gate of the Practice of the Banner of Great Compassion.
The third spiritual friend was the supreme elder Joyful City. He presided over all the Buddhas’ dharmas attained through dedication.
His liberation door was named "The Cultivation of the Pure Dharma of a Bodhisattva Reaching All Places."
The fourth spiritual friend was the bhikṣuṇī Siṃhavijṛmbhitā of the city of Kaliṅavana; she presided over the dedication toward reaching all places.
The dharma-gate she attained is named "The Gate of Liberation that Accomplishes All-Knowledge.
The fifth spiritual friend was the woman Vāsudhārā of the land of Durgama; she presided over the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit. The dharma-gate she attained...
The sixth gate is the liberation gate named "The Bodhisattva’s Transcendence of the Limit of Desire.
The sixth spiritual friend is the householder Viśuddhara of the City of Good Crossing, who presides over the dedication of all roots of goodness in accordance with firmness.
The liberation gate he has attained is named "The Bodhisattva’s Liberation that All Buddhas Never Enter Parinirvāṇa. The seventh spiritual friend is... [Supplement]... 補 (Bhu).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Mount To-lo (Dharaṇa) presides over the dedication that accords with all sentient beings;

the dharma-gate he has attained is named the "Liberation Gate of the Practice of Great Compassion. The eighth spiritual friend, the Bodhisattva Samantagāmin, presides over the dedication to the marks of True Suchness (Tathatā);
the dharma-gate he has attained is named the "Liberation Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Universal and Swift Practice."
The ninth spiritual friend is the great celestial deity of the city of Śrāvastī, who presides over the dedication of liberation that is unbound and unattached.

The dharma-gate he has attained is named the "Cloud-Net Liberation Gate. The tenth spiritual friend is the deity Abiding in the Site of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), who presides over the immeasurable dedication equal to the dharma-realm. The dharma-gate he has attained is named "Indestructible."
The liberation door of the treasury of wisdom. The above ten spiritual friends preside over the dharma-gates of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
The efficacy of practicing these dharmas shall be clarified by the sūtra itself hereafter.
The forty-first Dharma-gate: The Ten Good Spiritual Friends. The first good spiritual friend is the night goddess Vasanti of the city of Kapilavastu;

she presides over the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The Dharma-gate she has attained is named "The Liberation Gate of the Radiance of Dharma that Shatters the Darkness of Ignorance of All Sentient Beings. The second good spiritual friend is Bodhimanda-sarvaprāpta...

The Night Goddess Pure Light presides over the Ground of Freedom from Defilement; the Dharma-door she has attained is named "The Liberation Door of the Bodhisattva’s Joyful and Skillful Progression through Tranquil Meditative Concentration.
The third spiritual friend, the Night Goddess Joyfully Observing Sentient Beings on the right side of the Bodhimanda, presides over the Ground of Radiant Light;
the Dharma-door she has attained is named "The Liberation Door of the Universal Banner of Joy."
The fourth spiritual friend in this assembly of the virtuous is the Night Goddess Subhūṣitā Praśāntarutasāgaravatī, who presides over the stage of Radiant Intelligence (*Arciṣmatī*).
The liberation door she has attained is called "The Bodhisattva Liberation Door of Universally Manifesting in All Worlds to Discipline Sentient Beings.
The fifth spiritual friend, not far from here, is the Night Goddess Śāntamaticarandharasāgaravatī, who presides over...
The Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*). The Dharma-door attained is named the Liberation Door of the Vast Adornment of Great Joy Arising Moment by Moment.
The sixth spiritual friend is the Night Goddess Guardian of All City Lords within the Assembly of the Tathāgata;
she presides over the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī*). The Dharma-door attained is named the Liberation Door of the Profound, Sovereign, and Wondrous Sound. The seventh spiritual friend...
The night goddess Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasukhasaṃvāsā, who presides over the Stage of Far-Reaching (Dūramgamā),
has attained a dharma-door called the Bodhisattva’s Liberation Door of the Radiance of Vast Joy Born of Great Delight.
The eighth spiritual friend in this circle of the site of enlightenment is the night goddess Mahāpraṇidhānavīryaprabhāsarvasattvatrāṇī, who presides over the Immovable Stage (Acalā).
The Dharma door attained is named the "Gate of Liberation for Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings to Cause Them to Generate Roots of Goodness.

The ninth is the Night Goddess Wondrous Virtue of Perfect Radiance (*Lambinīvana-sundaraprabhā*), who possesses excellent wisdom and presides over the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
The Dharma-door attained is called "The Bodhisattva’s Gate of Liberation of Sovereign Manifestation of Birth Throughout All Places for Immeasurable Eons.
The tenth spiritual friend was Gopā, daughter of the King of Kapilavastu, who presides over the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
The Dharma-door she attained is called "The Gate of Liberation of Contemplating the Ocean of Samādhis of Bodhisattvas. These are the ten aforementioned [spiritual friends].
The functions of the practices for the ten stages of the Good Spiritual Friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) will be clarified later in the sutra itself.
Regarding the fifty-first dharma-gate, the ten Good Spiritual Friends:

the first is Māyādevī in this world, who presides over the gate of attaining Buddhahood through the illusory manifestation arising from compassion and wisdom. The dharma-gate she has attained is named "The Great [Vow] of the Bodhisattva."

He personally realized each of these meritorious practices, vows, and powers, so that they might serve as a model for the practice of sentient beings with great resolve in future generations.

Regarding the format: this is why the youth Sudhana addressed the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), saying, "I have previously resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should study the bodhisattva conduct (*caryā*) and cultivate the bodhisattva path (*mārga*).

By means of the ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), and ten stages (*bhūmi*), one traverses each of these four types of stages through the power of merit, practice, and vows.

Upon reaching the eleventh stage, the position of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one attains perfection through the effortless power of the ten great Dharma-gates; merit is complete and the fruit is fulfilled.

This samādhi is named "The Tathāgata-vairocana-garbha-body of All Buddhas," which universally enters all Buddhas.
Because of its equality, it can manifest all manner of images within the dharma-realm; vast and unimpeded, it is identical to space.
It enters into every whirlpool of the ocean of the dharma-realm without exception, giving rise to all samādhi dharmas.

It universally encompasses the dharma-realm of the ten directions, and the ocean of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is born from this. All that exists in the ten directions...
They are able to manifest all oceans of established realms; they contain within them all the powers of the Buddhas, the liberations, and the wisdoms of all Bodhisattvas.
They can cause all atoms of every land to universally accommodate the infinite Dharma-realm.
They accomplish the ocean of all Buddha-merits and reveal the ocean of all Tathāgatas’ great vows. [They encompass] all the wheels of Dharma possessed by all Buddhas.
May this be circulated and upheld so that it remains uninterrupted. Just as the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra entered this samādhi before the World-Honored One in this world,
so too throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space— in the ten directions and the three periods of time— is there the subtle, unimpeded,
and vast radiance seen by the Buddha-eye, reached by the Buddha’s power, and manifested by the Buddha-body in all lands.
The earth, as well as all the atoms within this land—in each and every atom, there are Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds;
in each and every field, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds;
and before each and every Buddha, there are Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds—all of whom likewise enter into this Vairocana of all Buddhas.
The Vairocana-Tathāgata-Garbha-Kāya Samādhi. At that time, before each and every Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, all the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared.
Those Tathāgatas spoke in unison, praising him: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are able to enter this Vairocana-Tathāgata-Garbha-Bodhi of all Buddhas."

"Sattvasamādhi! Son of the Buddha, this is because all the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively empower you, by virtue of the power of Vairocana Tathāgata’s original vows, and also by virtue of the power of your own cultivation of the practices and vows of all Buddhas."
Yet he was able to enter this samādhi in order to cause you to preach the Dharma and turn the Great Wheel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there were two assemblies; in the assembly where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī preached the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths, he did not enter meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there were three assemblies. At the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes was expounded.
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means.

By the power of this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions, there appeared Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-lands.
They were all of one name, called Dharmamati. They appeared before him and addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to enter this bodhisattva samādhi of immeasurable skillful means. Son of good family..."
Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-lands in each of the ten directions all empower you together through their spiritual powers.
Furthermore, by virtue of the power of the former vows of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the power of his majestic majesty, and the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated,
you have entered this samādhi and are enabled to preach the Dharma, so that the wisdom of the Buddhas may increase and you may penetrate deeply into the Dharma.
Because of the realms. Furthermore, he is endowed with ten kinds of knowledge. Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena is such through the power of this samādhi.

At that time, each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Dharmamati. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati arose from his meditative concentration.
He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha, the dwelling places of bodhisattvas are vast and equal to the dharma-realm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes, as fully detailed in the sutra itself.
Furthermore, there were four assemblies. In the palace of the Yāma Heaven, the Dharma-door of the Ten Practices was taught.
Bodhisattva Guṇakara, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation.

Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand buddha-fields, all of whom were named Guṇa.
The forest manifested before him and addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, saying: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to enter this Samādhi of Skillful Contemplation.

Good son, this is because all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions—numbering as many as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name—have collectively bestowed their empowerment upon you.
Furthermore, it is through the power of the vows made by the Tathāgata Vairocana in the past."

By the power of the deities and the power of the roots of goodness of the assembly of bodhisattvas, you have been enabled to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma, for the sake of increasing buddha-wisdom and for the sake of penetrating deeply into the dharma-realm. Furthermore, ten kinds of wisdom shall be bestowed upon you. Why is this?
Because the nature of the dharma of this samādhi power is thus, at that time each of the Buddhas extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the head of Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.
Then, Bodhisattva Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha immediately arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of the Buddha!"

The bodhisattva practice is inconceivable and equal to the dharma-realm. The Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma-vyūha then expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices, as fully contained within the sutra itself.
In the fifth assembly, at the Tuṣita Heaven palace, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications. The Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power...

[He] entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom. Having entered this samādhi, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared before him a hundred thousand Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields, all bearing the same name:
Vajradhvaja. They all spoke in praise, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
Thus you are able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom.
Good son, this is because the spiritual powers of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in a hundred thousand Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions collectively empower you.
It is also due to the power of the vows and the majestic spiritual authority of the Tathāgata Vairocana, as well as the purity of your own wisdom. All the Bodhisattvas...

Because their roots of goodness have increased and become preeminent, these Buddhas cause you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma, so that all bodhisattvas may attain pure fearlessness and be endowed with unimpeded eloquence.

At that time, the Buddhas immediately bestow immeasurable wisdom upon the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja, as well as ten kinds of immeasurable great Dharma-gates. Why is this? Because he has entered [this samādhi].
By the power of the roots of goodness of this samādhi, at that time each of the Buddhas stroked the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja with their right hand.
Having received this stroking of the head, the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja immediately arose from meditative concentration and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses inconceivable great vows that fill the Dharma-realm and are universally able to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
He then expounds the ten methods of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), as fully detailed in the sutra itself.
Furthermore, in the sixth assembly, in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages was taught.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
Having entered this samādhi, immediately, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten billion buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there were [ten billion buddha-fields... outside each.
Numerous Buddhas, all named Vajragarbha, appeared before him and spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!
You are indeed able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
Son of Good Family, these are the Buddhas of ten billion Buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within them, who together empower you through the Vairocana..."
By the power of the original vows of the Tathāgata Vairocana, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; by the power of your own supreme wisdom;

and because the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha has praised and expounded this vast and boundless Dharma-gate to attain great wisdom—at that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their right hand and stroked the crown of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha’s head. Having thus stroked his head, Vajra...
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "O sons of the Buddha!

The vows of the bodhisattvas are well-determined, unadulterated, and invisible. They are as vast as the Dharma-realm, as ultimate as space, extending to the end of the future, pervading all buddha-fields, and providing protection for all sentient beings for the sake of all [beings]."

Protected by the Buddha, he entered the wisdom of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and immediately expounded the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), as detailed in the sutra itself.
This consists of seven assemblies. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Aranya-dharma Bodhimanda in the kingdom of Magadha. At the beginning...
Having attained perfect enlightenment, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, he entered the Buddhas’ samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
By means of the sovereign power of his supernatural faculties of omniscience, he manifested the body of a Tathāgata— pure and unobstructed,
without dependence and free from objective clinging, abiding in śamatha, supremely tranquil, endowed with great majesty and virtue, untainted by attachment, and capable of causing others to see it.
They all attained awakening and manifested according to what was appropriate, never missing the proper time, while constantly abiding in the single mark— namely, the markless—
and were accompanied by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, all of whom had entered the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*),
were fully endowed with the practices of a Bodhisattva, and had attained the universal vision of Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless Dharma-realm.
Samādhi; great compassion and peace; mastery of supernatural powers equal to those of the Tathāgata for all sentient beings;
profound wisdom that expounds the true meaning; possession of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); subduing all Māras;

causing the Bodhisattvas to speak the Chapter on the Ten Samādhis, the Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers, the Chapter on the Ten Endurances, the Chapter on the Lifespan, the Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas, and the Radiance of the Minor Marks.
The Chapter on the Ten Bodies and the Ocean of Marks; the Chapter on the Universal Worthy’s Conduct; the Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata;
the Chapter on the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Himself Speaking of Incalculable Numbers; and the Chapter on the Inconceivability of the Buddha—these constitute eleven chapters in total.
The eighth assembly. At the third assembly, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra entered a vast samādhi called "Adorned with Buddha-Flowers.

When he entered this samādhi, all worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways and eighteen manners, and a great sound issued forth that was heard by all without exception. Thereafter, he arose from the samādhi. Because of this...
The Dharma-gate of Two Hundred Questions by the Bodhisattva Prajñā. He addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha, please explain for us: what is the reliance of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva? What is the extraordinary perception? What is their practice?
What are their spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and so forth? There were two hundred such questions in this Dharma-gate. The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, with a single...
There are ten questions, answered with ten responses, totaling two thousand dharma-gates as fully detailed in the sutra itself.

In the ninth assembly, the Jeta Grove Assembly, at that time the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, took great compassion as his body, great compassion as his gateway, and great compassion as his head;
employing the dharma of great compassion as his skillful means, he pervaded [all things].
The void entered the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). Having entered this samādhi, all worlds were universally purified and adorned.
At that time, this great pavilion of magnificent array suddenly became vast and expansive, without limit or boundary;
its ground was of vajra, its surface covered with precious gems, and immeasurable jewel flowers and various maṇis were scattered everywhere throughout it.

It was filled with immeasurable varieties of jewels, serving as its adornment. At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, the Jeta Grove became equal in extent to empty space, precisely the same size as unspeakably many buddha-fields, each containing as many atoms as there are dust motes in unspeakably many buddha-lands.
It was adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels interspersed throughout, and unspeakable numbers of gems were spread across its ground. Trees...
Each of these various adornments numbered incalculable *asaṃkhyeya*s, extending throughout the ten directions in magnificent rows.
At that time, within the void above the Jeta Grove, there were likewise unspeakably many and inconceivable varieties of adornments.

They pervade empty space and fill the entire dharma-realm. Furthermore, there are unspeakably many great bodhisattvas who pervade empty space and fill the dharma-realm, each making offerings and each praising the Tathāgata Vairocana’s inexhaustible dharma-gates, boundless meritorious virtues, practices, and vows, as fully detailed in the sutra itself. This concludes the preceding section.
The names and characteristics of the seven locations and nine assemblies where the World-Honored One entered meditative absorption, the scope of the meditative states of the great bodhisattvas,

the adornments of their emergence from absorption and their preaching of the Dharma, and the ritual protocols for the various assemblies of Buddhas who bore witness to and certified the preaching of the Dharma— the general outline of these matters is fully contained within the sutra itself.

Furthermore, the Ten Mysterious Gates and the Six Phases encompass the perfect fusion of this entire scripture. It is layered upon layered, inexhaustible, inexhaustible, inexhaustible, and inexhaustible.
As for the Ten Mysterious Gates: first is the Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment and Correspondence;
it is like a single drop of seawater containing the flavors of a hundred rivers. Second is the Gate of Unobstructed Freedom between the Broad and the Narrow; as if within a single foot...

1. The Gate of the Mutual Interpenetration of the One and the Many Without Confusion: like a mirror reflecting images from a thousand *li* away. 2. The Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of the One, the Three, and the Many:
like a thousand lamps in a single room, where light intermingles with light. 3. The Gate of the Sovereign Identity of All Dharmas: like gold and its golden color, which are inseparable. 4.
The Gate of the Simultaneous Manifestation and Concealment of Mysteries: like a crescent moon in the autumn sky, where dark and bright appear side by side. 5. The Gate of Subtle Characteristics.
1. The Gate of Establishing the Vessel: Like a lapis lazuli jar containing many forest trees. 2. The Gate of the Realm of the Seven Indra-Nets:
Like two mirrors reflecting each other, transmitting radiance and mirroring one another. 3. The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding:
Like raising a fist or extending an arm—whatever meets the eye is the Way. 4. The Gate of Accomplishing the Distinctness of Dharmas Despite Temporal Separation: Like a dream of one and many.
Soaring for a hundred years: the tenth gate is the Gate of the Perfect Interfusion and Endowment of Primary and Secondary Aspects.
Just as all the stars bow toward the North Star, the abode of the seasons, these ten gates together encompass the perfect interfusion of the entire sutra.

Furthermore, regarding the six characteristics—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—from the perspective of principle (*li*): that one contains many is called the totality of principle; that many are not one is called the particularity of principle;
that they do not contradict one another is called the sameness of principle; that they do not overlap with one another is called the difference of principle;

that they are collectively accomplished is called the formation of principle; and that each abides in its own original nature is called the disintegration of principle. From the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), they act together...

A single dharma is called the "totality of phenomena" (*vastu-samagra*). All dharmas being distinct is called the "differentiation of phenomena" (*vastu-vibhinna*). Many kinds that are not different is called the "sameness of phenomena" (*vastu-sama*).

Each being distinct is called the "difference of phenomena" (*vastu-bhinna*). All dharmas being accomplished is called the "completion of phenomena" (*vastu-niṣpanna*). Not departing from their own positions is called the "destruction of phenomena" (*vastu-vināśa*).
Furthermore, just as it is with this pair of principle and phenomenon, so it is with the other nine pairs— teaching and meaning, object and wisdom,

practice and stage, cause and fruit, support and supported, essence and function, person and dharma, opposition and conformity, and response and resonance— as well as the ten dharma-realms, which comprise hundreds, thousands, and so forth.

The six characteristics [of the hundred thousand dharmas] may be understood by analogy with this. Qingliang’s Verse says: "One is many; this constitutes the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Many are not one;

this constitutes the particular characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The various classes are identical within themselves, thereby establishing difference (*anyatva*). Each essence is distinct, thereby manifesting sameness (*ekatva*)."

The principle of the arising and ceasing of the one and the many is subtle and perfected; abiding in its own dharma, it is eternally unconditioned. It cognizes only objects and is not the consciousness of phenomena.
By this expedient means, one realizes the One Vehicle. Furthermore, these six characteristics—by citing one, all are fully encompassed—just like a single pearl.
It has six holes pierced through its four sides and top and bottom; the holes are interconnected so that by entering through any single hole, one can draw out all the pearls.
Chan Master Zhiyi of the Fayan school composed a verse on this: "The meaning of the Six Characteristics in the Avataṃsaka: within the identical there is still difference.

If difference were separate from identity, it would entirely miss the intent of the Buddhas. By means of these six characteristics, the principle of the entire scripture is encompassed without obstruction.

The unimpededness of phenomena (*dharmānāvaraṇa*), the unimpededness of principle and phenomena (*dharmadharmānāvaraṇa*), and the unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmānāvaraṇa*). Infinite within the infinite, perfectly interfused within the perfectly interfused.
From this point upward, the establishment of the general headings and subheadings is complete.
Furthermore, regarding this Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean: it is the realm of true recompense and non-obstruction where the Tathāgata Vairocana resides.

It contains ten unspeakable numbers of fragrant water oceans, ten unspeakable numbers of world-systems, and twenty tiers of flower treasuries, all of which are contained within this Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.
They are arranged and situated within the ocean. Furthermore, I shall now set forth in order the names, characteristics, and numbers of the twenty tiers of the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.

Within the first tier of fragrant water-oceans at the very bottom of this world-system, there is a central world-germ (lokadhātu-jāti), surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
In this ocean, they are arranged and situated. In the second layer of the fragrant water ocean, there are worlds numbering as many as the atoms in two buddha-fields;
these are arranged and situated within this ocean. In the third layer of the fragrant water ocean, there are worlds numbering as many as the atoms in three buddha-fields;
these are arranged and situated within this ocean. In the fourth layer of the fragrant water...
Within this ocean, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in four buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this ocean.
Within the fifth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in five buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this ocean.
Within the sixth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in six buddha-fields. In...

Within this ocean, they are arranged and situated. Within the seventh layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in seven buddha-fields, which are arranged and situated within this ocean.

Within the eighth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in eight buddha-fields, which are arranged and situated within this ocean. Within the ninth layer of fragrant water oceans...
Within the [ninth] layer, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in nine buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this sea of fragrant water.
Within the tenth layer of the sea of fragrant water, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this sea of fragrant water.
Within the eleventh layer of the sea of fragrant water, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in eleven buddha-fields.

Within this ocean, they are arranged and abide. Within the twelfth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in twelve buddha-fields, which are arranged and abide within this ocean.
The thirteenth layer of fragrant water ocean is precisely the fragrant water ocean within this Sahā world, named Boundless Light of Exquisite Flowers. This...

This is the most central fragrant ocean. The most central world-system is named Sahā, which is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this ocean.
Within the fourteenth layer of fragrant oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in fourteen buddha-fields, situated within this ocean.
They are arranged and situated therein. In the fifteenth layer of the fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in fifteen buddha-fields;

they are arranged and situated within this ocean. In the sixteenth layer of the fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in sixteen buddha-fields; they are arranged and situated within this ocean. In the seventeenth layer...
Within the ocean of fragrant water, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in seventeen buddha-fields, arranged and situated within this ocean.
Within the eighteenth layer of the ocean of fragrant water, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in eighteen buddha-fields.
Within this ocean, they are arranged and abide. Within the nineteenth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in nineteen buddha-fields;

within this ocean, they are arranged and abide. Within the twentieth layer of fragrant water oceans, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in twenty buddha-fields; within this ocean, they are arranged and abide.
This is the first twenty-fold layer at the very center. It is explained in detail in this manner:
there are ten "unspeakables" (anabhilāpya) of these twenty-fold layers. How is one "unspeakable" constituted? For example, ten hundred thousand is one *koṭi*;
ten *koṭis* is one *niyuta*; ten *niyutas* is one *kaṅkara*; ten *kaṅkaras* is one *bimbara*. In this way, increasing by tens each time, it becomes one [unit].

The total count: thus it increases twofold at each step until the one hundred and twentieth great total count, which becomes inconceivable, ineffable, incomparable, and immeasurable; therefore, it is called "one unspeakable" (*asamkhyeya*).
Up to ten such great numbers, it is called "ten unspeakables," and is also termed the number of "ten *asaṃkhyeyas*."
Thus it is extensively explained that empty space is inexhaustible and the dharma-realm is boundless; in this way, they are layered upon one another, infinitely and inexhaustibly.
This is not something that ordinary minds can measure; only Buddhas and Buddhas can know it to its ultimate conclusion.
Furthermore, to discuss this thirteenth layer once more: the central fragrant water ocean is named Boundless Exquisite Flower Light Fragrant Water Ocean.
It is surrounded on its outer perimeter by ten water oceans that encircle the first central fragrant water ocean.
Additionally, there are one hundred fragrant water oceans that surround these eleven fragrant water oceans.
Thus it is explained in detail. There are ten unspeakable numbers of fragrant water oceans surrounding one another in successive layers.
Within each of these fragrant water oceans, worlds are arranged as previously described. In the very center, within the thirteenth layer of fragrant water oceans, [the central world is situated].
There are worlds as numerous as the atoms within thirteen buddha-fields arranged therein, abiding within this ocean.
As it is with one ocean, so it is with every ocean. This refers to the perimeter beyond the thirteenth layer.
Regarding the ten unspeakable numbers of fragrant water oceans, one should contemplate and realize the rest; in total, it is one great fragrance.
The ocean of water is likewise in one layer; it is also so in twenty layers. This is the first set of twenty concentric layers at the very center.
There are ten sets of twenty layers that surround this first central set of twenty layers.
Furthermore, there are one hundred sets of twenty layers that surround these eleven sets of twenty layers. Thus it is explained in detail.
There are ten unspeakable numbers of twenty-layered seas of fragrant water and ten unspeakable numbers of world-systems.

Furthermore, as for what constitutes these twenty layers: just as in the first layer, within this sea of fragrant water at the very bottom, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, arranged and situated within this sea. Within such worlds, there are...
There are four great continents, which are the four major islands; eight intermediate continents; and tens of thousands of minor islands.
At the very center is Mount Sumeru, surrounded on all sides by the Lesser Cakravāḍa Mountains. Below these are the earth wheel and the water wheel; the gold wheel is itself the fire wheel;
beneath the fire wheel is the wind wheel; and further below is empty space. Above the earth wheel, within this empty space, is the sun.
The moon and stars, and all that is empty, enter the celestial realms. This first tier of heavens is named Śakra-devānām-indra;
its formal name is Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Ascending one more tier is Yāma Heaven. Ascending again is Tuṣita Heaven. Ascending again is Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Ascending again is Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Proceeding upward in this sequence, one reaches the limit of the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
It reaches to the ends of the heavens. Above this, in the four directions, there is all empty space; these are also called the Four Heavens of Emptiness (*catasraḥ śūnyatā-deva-lokāḥ*).
Because it ceases here, it is termed a single layer of world and a single layer of heaven and earth. As for its breadth, from east to west, it measures seven hundred and twenty thousand *li*.
It extends sixty-four thousand li from north to south. Its height rises from the earth's surface up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Ultimate Form Heaven).
The Abhidharma-śāstra states: "If one were to drop a massive mountain of stone from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven down to the land of Jambudvīpa..."

Sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-five seasons—four seasons constituting one year—amount, when calculated in total, to sixteen thousand five hundred and eighty-three years and three additional seasons. Such is its sublime height.
Furthermore, regarding the earth wheel (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*), its thickness is sixty-eight thousand *yojana*s.
Calculated by conversion, this amounts to five hundred and forty-four million *li*. Moreover, the water wheel (*jala-maṇḍala*) is eighty thousand *yojana*s high;
together, their depth and breadth total six trillion four hundred billion *li*, which is one million two hundred thousand three thousand four hundred and fifty *yojana*s.
One *yojana* is calculated using the great *yojana*, totaling nine trillion, six hundred and twenty-seven million six thousand *li*.

Furthermore, the gold wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*) is identical to the fire wheel (*tejo-maṇḍala*), standing thirty-two thousand *yojanas* high; by calculation, this totals two million five hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
Moreover, the wind wheel (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) stands one million six hundred thousand *yojanas* high, which calculates to one hundred... [million *li*].

It measures twenty-eight *zhào* (one *zhào* being one million *mǐ*) in length. Such dimensions—its height, breadth, and width—are called one layer of fragrant water-ocean and one world-system (*lokadhātu-jāti*).
This constitutes one layer of heaven and earth, and one layer of the four wheels of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Regarding such calculations of layers, starting from the first layer at the very bottom, there are likewise a second, third, and fourth layer.
Layer Thirteen: Herein lies the most central region of the upper [levels]. The fragrant ocean is named Boundless Wondrous Flower, and the world-system is named Sahā.
Furthermore, from the fourteenth layer up to the twentieth layer, the fragrant oceans and world-systems consist of the four wheels of wind, fire, water, and earth. This is the first pair.
The ten layers, their sequence, and their names are explained in detail as follows:

The Principle-Dharmadhātu:

Principle is the essence of phenomena (dharma), and phenomena are the function of principle. Essence and function are both manifested together. "Dhātu" (realm) signifies the limit; principle is fundamentally pure.
Phenomena arise through the realization of principle; principle and phenomena are one. What need is there to wait for anything that is not true?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Dharma-realm pervades all transformations; the One and the Principle are harmonized. (As the verse states:
"The essential nature is perfectly luminous, and the meaning of the Principle is manifest; The pure Dharma-realm is not spatially limited.
True Suchness possesses jewel-like marks, empty, luminous, and tranquil; The Great Void does not depart from the light of self-nature."

The Phenomenal Dharma-realm (*vastu-dharmadhātu*). The phenomena of the realm are manifested through causes and conditions; The creation of dharmas arises from the mind. The realms define their respective positions; Together they support the beauty of Bodhi.
Phenomena originally have no mind of their own; They exist because of objects. When phenomena accord with principle, The realms attain their proper fitness.
Therefore, a sutra says: "When phenomena and principle are thoroughly penetrated, all dharmas are unimpeded" (the verse says):
Whether phenomena are large or small, round or square, One attains the source and bottom of the Dharma, where the nature is pure and cool.
Confronting objects, they arise as illusory existences through the mind; Through the union and separation of causes and conditions, each asserts its own claim.
The dharma-realm of principle and phenomena: principle and phenomena constitute three aspects; the general and the particular each take precedence. The realm serves as the boundary and limit.
These dharmas establish themselves as three distinct matters. Dharmas have no fixed characteristics, and the realms are likewise intermingled; phenomena have no single certainty.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All arise because of the unconditioned dharma, yet there are distinctions" (as the verse states):
The three factors are mutually integrated; the dharma has no differentiation. Principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused; the dharma-nature is vast.
All dharmas are like the meaning of emptiness, the dharma-realm; There is no person, no self, and no teaching of dharmas.

phenomena and phenomena interpenetrate; phenomena and phenomena are perfectly interfused. The dharma-realm is established, and the mind finds its place within it.
Each phenomenon presides over its own sphere, serving as the balance and the guiding principle. The dharma-realm is thus, and its self-nature is thus.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The true mark is markless; the dharma-realm is a provisional name. (As the verse says:
"Each phenomenon penetrates all others, for the principle is thus: Returning the mind to its source, one attains mastery in contemplating the void dharma-realm as it returns to the ocean of nature;
In every dust mote and every land, every dharma is perfectly complete."

In the non-obstruction of phenomena, each and every dharma is perfectly interfused, melting into a single unity, with the One threading through them all.

It is thus with the Dharma-realm; it is thus with empty space; it is thus with self-nature; and it is thus with principle as well. The true emptiness is the Dharma-realm, and the Dharma-realm is true emptiness.

Both are gathered and both are released, subsumed and returned to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The nature of this limit of reality is emptiness, its measure equal to the Dharma-realm. Therefore, it is said: "The three realms are but..."
The mind is the sole reality of all phenomena; contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm in stillness. All things are created solely by the mind. How, then, are they created by the mind alone?
Indeed, the entire Dharma-realm is manifested through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These four great elements undergo formation and disintegration, arising and ceasing.
All these arise from the mind and its mental concomitants; they are subject to arising and ceasing without abiding, and their movements are incessant, thus resulting in saṃsāra.

Through the combination of the four great elements, the world is formed; through the dispersal and extinction of the four great elements, the world is destroyed. Thus, formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness cycle endlessly.
For this reason, Śākyamuni Buddha, with his Buddha-eye, perceives the minds of others from afar and clearly discerns the great earth, mountains, and rivers.

In the lands as numerous as motes of dust, there are sentient and insentient beings; all things and all phenomena, heaven and earth, the people, the sun, moon, and stars, sovereigns and ministers, fathers and sons, the Odes, the Documents, the Rites, and the Music—all virtues are fully present therein. Furthermore, he observes sentient beings creating all manner of karmic actions.
They undergo various sufferings—birth, old age, sickness, and death—with no time of liberation. Having observed this, the Buddha suddenly gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
When the causal conditions and the time had arrived, he manifested a great supernormal transformation:
descending from the Tuṣita Heaven to the human realm, he entered the womb of Queen Māyā in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. After ten months, he was born; with a single cry, he walked seven paces.
He looked around in the four directions, pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, declaring: "In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am the most honored.
This was in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhou Zhao, the Jia-Yin year, on the eighth day of the fourth month at the hour of the rat.
At nineteen, he left home; at thirty, he attained enlightenment. He preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, delivering over three hundred assemblies of sutras. Heaven...
When human realization of the fruits of the path becomes clear and one attains full awakening, the merits and virtues of a single lifetime will be complete.

All the dharmas he expounds are for the sake of delivering all sentient beings; he preaches according to the faculties and natures of those beings. Prior to this, he employs a single mind to open up ten kinds of dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), discussing them repeatedly.
Regarding the essence, magnitude, and form of these dharma-realms, there are eight [distinctions] based on the minds of sentient beings.

Regarding the creation of the eighty-four thousand afflictions and their corresponding wholesome and unwholesome deeds, the Buddha opened eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of skillful means (*upāya*).
Through various skillful means, causal conditions, parables, and modes of expression, he expounded them extensively.
Administering medicine according to the disease, he enabled all sentient beings to sever and extinguish the manifold maladies of birth and death, so that their bodies and minds might find peace.

They joyfully realize the fruits of the Way; because they are all brought to final liberation through *nirvāṇa*, the world is discussed in terms of the *dharmadhātu*, wherein there is no dharma that is not complete.
Furthermore, the *dharmadhātu* is discussed in terms of the world, wherein there is no phenomenon that does not fully encompass the Dharma.
Because the Dharma is thus complete and every phenomenon is entirely pervasive, it is called the Great *Dharmadhātu*. Thus, a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: Vairocana...
The wondrous body pervades the Dharma-realm, serving as the Flower Treasury Adornment; it is equal to the great void, its measure being only itself. Furthermore, a verse says:
"The mental capacities of atoms within all lands may be counted; the water in the great oceans may be drunk up; space may be measured and the wind may be bound;
yet none can exhaustively praise the Buddha’s merits. It also says: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, [and mirages]."

"Reflections are like dew and like lightning; one should contemplate them in this way. For this reason, though my own knowledge is shallow and my wisdom dull, I have not hesitated to disregard my own meager and flawed understanding.
I shall discuss these four dharmas according to their general course, briefly outlining their broad outlines regarding names, characteristics, phenomena, and principle, in a single enumeration.
I pray that those of wise intellect will further elucidate and clarify them for the sake of the future, so as to broaden the scope of what is seen and heard, and bring about awakening.
This was composed by the śramaṇas Yong-gwang and Jeong-quan of Guangde Temple in Suī County, who have attained great eloquence through the nature of wisdom.
